DESIGN & EVIDENCE

Follow one order.
Check every effect.

The job

A store operator needs to explain contribution changes, find products with refund exposure, measure observed repeat purchase and identify cash collection/refund gaps. This is an accounting and reconciliation system. It does not predict growth or claim that advertising caused sales.

The data flow

Canonical store export → typed validation and atomic ingestion → separate orders, items, payment events, refund grants and advertising → dbt financial models → tests → read-only evidence snapshot.

Why the modelling matters

Two items and two payment captures are four rows if joined directly. That can double sales or fees. Here, line totals and payment fees are aggregated independently before joining to an order. A refund grant reduces revenue; its payment return reduces cash. Those two events may occur on different dates.

Why late data works

Every newly accepted event receives an ingestion batch number. Incremental models recompute affected orders, lines, products and reporting periods, even when the business event is months old. The watermark advances only after dbt tests pass. Exact replays create no new source rows. Small acquisition and retention summaries rebuild so historical first purchases cannot leave stale cohorts.

What has been tested

Multi-item orders; split and failed payments; partial collections; partial line refunds; refunds returned later; duplicate delivery; invalid joins; conflicting IDs; rollback; quoted multiline data; late historical events; full-refresh equivalence; and failure without watermark advancement. See the tests and recorded raw benchmark outputs in GitHub.

What this does not prove

No real store is connected. No business uplift, universal connector, production SLA, arbitrary currency support or independent developer proficiency is claimed. The implementation was AI-assisted. Sarfaraz must be able to explain and change these rules independently; an interview exercise is included in the source.
